\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Quality floor}: $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(b) \geq \tau$.
  Convergence under contaminated training improves with the effective real fraction~\citep{wang2026survive}; $\tau$ sets the minimum acceptable quality level.
  By Proposition~\ref{prop:monotone}, this constraint defines a \emph{lower bound} $b_\tau = \inf\{b \geq 0 : \alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(b) \geq \tau\}$.
  \item \textbf{Stability ceiling}: $\mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq n_{\min}$.
  Overly concentrated weights yield high-variance gradients; $n_{\min}$ prevents the batch from degenerating into a single effective sample.
  Since $\mathrm{ESS}$ is decreasing, this defines an \emph{upper bound} $b_{\mathrm{ESS}} = \sup\{b \geq 0 : \mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq n_{\min}\}$.
\end{enumerate}
The optimal exponent is
\begin{equation}
  b^{*} = \inf\bigl\{b \geq 0 : \alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(b) \geq \tau\bigr\} \;\;\text{s.t.}\;\; \mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq n_{\min}.
  \label{eq:bstar}
\end{equation}
This is an empirically motivated \emph{minimum intervention} design choice: apply the smallest $b$ that achieves the quality floor.
Borderline samples (those with moderate $q$-values) still carry useful training signal; over-downweighting discards this signal unnecessarily.
When both constraints are satisfiable ($b_\tau \leq b_{\mathrm{ESS}}$), $b^{*} = b_\tau$ and $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the binding constraint, and $b^{*}$ lies well below the ESS ceiling.
When they conflict ($b_\tau > b_{\mathrm{ESS}}$), the stability ceiling takes precedence: $b^{*} = b_{\mathrm{ESS}}$, accepting a lower $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ to preserve gradient stability.
The three regimes (clean, $\aeff$-binding, ESS-binding) partition the training batches; we quantify their relative frequencies in \S\ref{sec:regime}.

\subsection{Algorithm}
\label{sec:algorithm}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:bstar} computes $b^{*}$ for each training batch.
At our micro-batch size $B{=}4$, $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ takes only five discrete values $\{0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0\}$; bisection finds the correct threshold but the landscape is discrete, not continuous.
The analytical contributions (epoch confound, detector type effects) hold independent of $B$; adaptive $\bstar$ is validated at $B \in \{4, 8, 16\}$ with PPL differences ${<}0.01$ (Appendix~\ref{app:alpha_validation}).
Each batch falls into one of three regimes:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Clean} ($\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(0) \geq \tau$): the quality floor holds at $b = 0$; no reweighting needed.
  \item \textbf{$\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$-binding} ($b_\tau \leq b_{\mathrm{ESS}}$): the quality constraint determines $b^{*} = b_\tau$; $\mathrm{ESS}$ remains above $n_{\min}$ with margin.
  \item \textbf{ESS-binding} ($b_\tau > b_{\mathrm{ESS}}$): the stability ceiling caps $b^{*} = b_{\mathrm{ESS}}$.

Because synthetic documents are shorter on average (304 vs.\ 560 words), the document-level synthetic fraction is 55.6\% at $\rho{=}0.4$.}
This self-contamination design means generator and trainee share the same distribution; implications for detection difficulty are discussed in \S\ref{sec:limitations}.

\paragraph{Detector.}
We train a TF-IDF + Logistic Regression classifier on a held-out labeled split (AUC\,=\,0.94, calibrated ECE\,=\,0.05 after temperature scaling with $T{=}0.204$).
The resulting $q$-scores have mean 0.60, standard deviation 0.37, and median 0.71, with 46.3\% of samples in the uncertain range $[0.2, 0.8]$.
We use this lightweight detector rather than neural alternatives (e.g., ModernBERT at AUC\,${\geq}$\,0.98 in \citealt{drayson2025detection}) to test whether score \emph{calibration} may matter as much as raw discrimination for reweighting.
To evaluate detector sensitivity, we additionally test two generative baselines: a GPT-2-based perplexity scorer (AUC\,=\,0.91) and an N-gram language model perplexity scorer (AUC\,=\,0.73); results are reported in \S\ref{sec:robustness}.

\paragraph{Training.}
We continue pretraining Qwen3-0.6B from its pretrained weights for 6{,}103 steps (batch size 4, gradient accumulation 4, effective batch 16) with AdamW, cosine schedule (peak lr\,=\,$5{\times}10^{-5}$), max sequence length 2048, and bf16 precision on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (96\,GB).

  \item \textbf{Adaptive} (ours): per-batch $b^*$ from the dual-constraint formulation (\S\ref{sec:method}), with $\tau = 0.8$ and $n_{\min} = 2$ (half the micro-batch size).

The detect-and-reweight paradigm~\citep{drayson2025detection} has emerged as a response to synthetic contamination in web corpora, now estimated at 20--60\% of crawled data~\citep{cheng2025contamination}.
Training on such data risks model collapse~\citep{shumailov2024model,dohmatob2025strong}, motivating methods that downweight likely-synthetic samples via $w(x) = (1 - q(x))^b$, where $q(x)$ is a detector's synthetic probability.
An alternative, Detect and Remove (D\&R), hard-filters samples above a threshold~\citep{feng2025beyond}.

Despite growing adoption, fundamental questions remain.
Does D\&R genuinely outperform soft reweighting, or do published comparisons confound filtering quality with multi-epoch exposure?
How should $b$ be chosen, given that \citet{drayson2025detection} find optimal values ranging from $b{=}10$ (GPT-2 124M) to $b{=}1$ (SmolLM 1.7B), requiring costly per-model grid search?
What detector properties are necessary for effective reweighting?

We investigate these questions through controlled experiments on Qwen3-0.6B continued pretraining (132M FineWeb tokens, $\rho{=}0.4$, 3 seeds), with extensions to $\rho \in \{0.2, 0.6\}$ and 1.7B parameters.\footnote{Our scope is continued pretraining on moderate-scale corpora with known contamination~\citep{gururangan2020dont}; generalization to from-scratch pretraining at web scale is untested.}
For the exponent selection problem, we derive $b$ per-batch from a dual-constrained formulation: find the minimum $b$ such that the weighted effective real proportion $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(b) \geq \tau$ (quality floor, motivated by convergence theory~\citep{wang2026survive}), subject to Kish's effective sample size $\mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq n_{\min}$ (stability ceiling)~\citep{kish1965survey,vehtari2024psis}.

Our analysis identifies two evaluation confounds and characterizes adaptive reweighting:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item \textbf{Epoch confound.}
D\&R's PPL advantage is entirely attributable to multi-epoch exposure; epoch-matched controls ($N{=}3$) reduce the gap to $\Delta{=}0.006$ (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_match}).

\item \textbf{Distribution matching.}
The in-distribution improvement ($\Delta{=}{-}0.043$ on FineWeb) does not transfer out-of-distribution (OpenWebText $+$0.06, Wikipedia $+$0.14; \S\ref{sec:robustness}).

\item \textbf{Adaptive reweighting characterization.}
The dual-constrained $\bstar$ matches grid-search performance without per-model tuning ($\Delta{=}{-}0.043$ vs.\ uniform, directionally consistent across seeds; gap to grid-best 0.031, 95\% CI $[-0.039, 0.101]$; Table~\ref{tab:main}).
The $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ quality constraint binds in 38.2\% of batches at 4.9$\times$ lower exponents than an ESS-only alternative (\S\ref{sec:regime}).
Detector signal type may matter more than discrimination accuracy: two generative detectors reverse the advantage (3 detectors, single seed; \S\ref{sec:robustness}).
The method fails at $\rho{=}0.2$ and shows no effect at 1.7B.
\end{itemize}
